items.title: [RFC] OpenSearch Memory API: events and memories for AI agents
items.body:
## What are you proposing?

Agent memory has evolved rapidly across the industry. Agents used to keep a chat history. More and more, they keep facts, summaries, and preferences that a large language model (LLM) extracts from conversations, carry them across sessions and agents, and act on them. As memory moves from a log of messages to knowledge an agent relies on, applications need three things that today's memory APIs do not give together:

- **Lineage.** Knowing which conversation each memory came from, so it can be checked, corrected, or deleted with its source.
- **Configurability.** Choosing, for each application, what gets extracted, with which prompt and model, how long raw records and memories are kept, and who can read and change them.
- **The raw record.** Keeping the original conversation searchable, because extraction leaves details out.

This RFC proposes a new memory API for OpenSearch, under `/_plugins/_memory`, built around those needs. It stores two kinds of records in a **Space**, which holds an application's extraction strategies, models, expiry settings, and access:

- **Events.** What an agent or application writes: conversation turns, agent state, tool results, or any JSON document. Events are kept as written and never change.
- **Memories.** What an LLM extracts from events in the background: facts, session summaries, user preferences, or whatever a custom prompt asks for. Each memory records the events it came from. An application can also write memories it extracts itself.

The API is **experimental**: it is off unless a cluster turns it on with a static setting, and it can change between releases until the community agrees it is stable. This RFC does not decide where the code lives. It could be part of the ML Commons plugin, or a dedicated plugin that calls ML Commons for models, as the Neural Search plugin does; the API design does not depend on the answer.

## What problems are you trying to solve?

An agent's memory holds two kinds of records: what happened, such as conversation turns, tool results, and agent state, and what an LLM inferred from it, such as facts, summaries, and preferences. The two need different rules. Raw records should never change, while inferred ones are updated as new turns refine them. They need their own lifetimes and their own permissions. Each inference also needs a link back to the records it came from, so a detail it left out can still be found, and so it can be deleted with its conversation. Agentic memory does not keep the two apart, as the next section shows. This RFC makes them two resources, events and memories, linked by lineage.

## Why events and memories are separate resources

An event is something that happened. A memory is something an LLM inferred from what happened. The two differ in who writes them, whether they can change, how long they are kept, and how they are found:

|  | Event | Memory |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A raw record: a conversation turn, agent state, a tool result, or a JSON document | An inference: a fact, a summary, a preference, or the output of a custom prompt |
| Who writes it | The agent or application | The extraction pipeline, or the application with CreateMemory |
| How it is made | Stored exactly as sent | An LLM call, which is not deterministic |
| Can it change? | No | Yes. Consolidation updates it when new events refine it, and the application can update or delete it |
| How long it is kept | Usually short: days to months (`event_expiry_days`) | Usually long: months to years, or forever (`memory_expiry_days`) |
| Typical size | A whole turn or document | A sentence or a paragraph |
| How it is found | By session and time, by ID, or by keyword and vector search over its chunks | By keyword and vector search, filtered by actor and strategy |

The relationship between them is many to many:

- One event can produce several memories of different types, for example a fact, an updated session summary, and a user preference.
- One event can produce no new memory, when consolidation finds that existing memories already cover it.
- One memory can come from several events, when consolidation merges what they said.

**Lineage.** Every memory records the events it came from in `source_event_ids`. That link supports a two-step retrieval pattern. An agent searches memories first, which returns a few short records instead of whole conversations. If a memory lacks the detail the agent needs, such as the exact error message or the full list a user gave, the agent follows `source_event_ids` to the original events. The link also works the other way: a memory search can filter by `source_event_ids`, so an application can find every memory that came from given events and delete them. Events are usually kept for less time than the memories made from them; once an event is deleted, BatchGetEvent reports its ID as not found.

**How agentic memory models this.** Agentic memory in ML Commons keeps both under one memory container API, with the raw records as one memory type (working memory) and the extracted records as another (long-term memory), next to sessions and history. The same paths and fields then serve records with different lifetimes and rules: working memory can be edited after it is written, and a long-term memory does not reference the messages it came from.

Agent memory systems commonly call these two kinds of records short-term memory and long-term memory. In this API, short-term memory is events, and long-term memory is memories.

## Why a new API, and how it relates to agentic memory

The ML Commons plugin has two memory APIs today: conversation memory and agentic memory. Given that conversation memory is on the deprecation path ([maintainer comment on ml-commons#4552](https://github.com/opensearch-project/ml-commons/issues/4552#issuecomment-3844465824)), this RFC mainly compares the new memory API with agentic memory. The section "Long-term direction: one memory API" describes the proposal to converge on one.

Agentic memory (experimental in 3.2, generally available in 3.3, `/_plugins/_ml/memory_containers`) stores messages in memory containers and extracts long-term memories from them. ML Commons agents use it, and other applications can call it directly.

Another API has a real cost: more code to maintain, and more for users to choose between. We propose it because the event and memory model changes the data model of agentic memory, not just its features:

- **Two record types instead of four.** Agentic memory has sessions, working memory, long-term memory, and history, each under the same generic paths. Splitting them into events and memories changes its paths.
- **Raw records that never change.** Agentic memory's working memory can be updated. Making it immutable breaks callers that update it.
- **Fixed actor and session fields on every record.** Agentic memory scopes records with namespace keys that each strategy chooses, such as `user_id`. A strategy whose key is missing from a write is skipped. Replacing namespaces with two fixed fields changes every request and response.
- **A link from every memory to its events.** This part is additive, and agentic memory could add it on its own.

Changing agentic memory this way would break its current users, including ML Commons agents. A new, experimental API leaves both existing APIs as they are, and lets the new model prove itself before anything is deprecated.

The table compares the three:

| Area | Memory API (proposed) | Agentic memory | Conversation memory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Containers and records | A Space holds events and memories | A memory container holds four memory types: sessions, working, long-term, and history | A memory holds one conversation's messages, each an input and a response, with optional traces |
| User and session | Every event and memory has an `actor_id` and an optional `session_id` | Each strategy names the namespace keys it needs, for example `user_id`, or `agent_id` and `session_id` | One memory per conversation, owned by the OpenSearch user who created it |
| Long-term memories | Extracted by an LLM, or written by the client | Extracted by an LLM | None |
| Source of a memory | Each memory records `source_event_ids`, and memory search can filter by them | Not recorded | Not applicable |
| Updating a raw record | No. Events cannot be changed | Yes, working memory can be updated | Yes, messages can be updated |
| Consolidation | Yes | Yes. For each new fact, the LLM decides to add, update, or delete against similar stored memories (`max_infer_size`, 5 by default, at most 10), and a history index records each change | Not applicable |
| Search over raw records | Keyword, semantic, and hybrid | Keyword only. Working memory is not embedded | Keyword only |
| Search over memories | Keyword, semantic, and hybrid | Keyword, semantic, and hybrid. Semantic queries since 3.3; dedicated semantic and hybrid APIs since 3.6 | Not applicable |
| Expiry | Per Space, for events and for memories. An expired memory is left out of reads before it is deleted | Since 3.8, with age and count limits and pinning. On-demand runs and a dry run since 3.9. An expired record is returned until the retention job deletes it | None |
| Strategies | SEMANTIC, SUMMARY, and CUSTOM | SEMANTIC, USER_PREFERENCE, and SUMMARY, each with an optional custom prompt | None |

The new API starts with a focused feature set. Features that agentic memory has, such as a change history, delete by query, per-request hybrid weights, count limits and pinning in retention, a built-in user-preference strategy, and checkpoint fields, can be added based on community interest.

**What changes in existing components:**

| Component | Change |
| --- | --- |
| ML Commons plugin | Either it hosts the new API, or it is called through its client for model predictions, as the Neural Search and Flow Framework plugins call it. Its two memory APIs do not change. With a dedicated plugin, it adds a memory type extension point for agents (see "Long-term direction") |
| Security plugin | None required. When it is installed, Spaces can be registered with its resource sharing framework |
| k-NN and Neural Search plugins | None. The k-NN plugin provides vector fields, and the Neural Search plugin provides the `text_chunking` processor and `neural` and `hybrid` queries |
| Job Scheduler plugin | None. The implementation registers its own jobs for the extraction backlog and for expiry |
| OpenSearch core | None |

## What is the developer experience going to be?

### Use cases

Some common use cases for the API:

- When an agent needs a detail from earlier turns, such as an error code, a file name, or a value a user gave, the agent developer wants to search the raw turns by keyword and by meaning, so the agent finds the exact detail even when no extracted memory kept it.
- When memories go stale or a retention rule applies, the developer wants events and memories to expire after a set time, so old memories stop shaping answers and data is not kept longer than allowed.
- When an agent resumes a session or restarts, the agent developer wants to reload the session's recent turns, so the conversation continues where it left off.
- When a user returns to an agent in a new session, the agent developer wants the agent to recall facts and preferences from earlier sessions, so the user does not repeat them.
- When a conversation runs long, the developer wants a running summary of the whole session, so the agent can keep context without sending every turn to the model.
- When an application serves more than one end user, the developer wants each end user's memories stored under that user's ID and searchable by user and session, so the application shows each user only their own memories.
- When an agent needs a detail a memory left out, or an application must show where a memory came from or delete what a conversation produced, the developer wants each memory linked to the events it came from, so the agent can read the original turns and the application can check or delete memories by their source.

### Experimental status

The API is off by default. A cluster turns it on with a static setting in `opensearch.yml`, for example `plugins.memory.experimental.enabled: true`. The final name follows from where the code lives. With the setting off, the memory paths do not exist.

While the API is experimental:

- It can change in breaking ways between releases. The release notes list every change, and any step needed for data written by an earlier release.
- The documentation marks it with one notice: "Experimental: this API can change between releases until it is marked stable."
- It does not replace or change the ML Commons memory APIs.

### Resources

- **Space.** A container for one application's memory. It holds the memory strategies, the ML Commons model used for extraction (`extraction_model_id`), the ML Commons model used for vectors (`embedding_model_id`), and how long to keep events (`event_expiry_days`, default 90) and memories (`memory_expiry_days`, default 365, where 0 means never). Without an extraction model, a Space stores events and extracts nothing. Without an embedding model, search is by keyword only. The embedding model cannot be changed after the Space is created, because stored vectors would no longer match. A Space with an embedding model also gives `embedding_dimension`, the size of the model's vectors.
- **Event.** One conversation turn, a group of turns, or a JSON document. An event has an actor ID (for example, the end user), an optional session ID, a timestamp, the payload, and string key-value pairs of metadata.
- **Memory.** A record extracted from events by a strategy, or written directly with CreateMemory. Each memory belongs to one strategy, one actor, and optionally one session, and records the events it came from in `source_event_ids`.

### Strategies

A strategy tells the extraction pipeline what to extract. Two types ship with built-in prompts, and `CUSTOM` brings its own:

| Type | What it extracts |
| --- | --- |
| `SEMANTIC` | Facts stated in the conversation, as short standalone statements |
| `SUMMARY` | One running summary per session, updated with each event |
| `CUSTOM` | Whatever the strategy's `extraction_prompt` asks for, for example user preferences |

On any strategy, `configuration.consolidation_enabled` turns consolidation with stored memories on or off. Strategies read a JSON event as JSON text.

### Operations

All paths are under `/_plugins/_memory`, whichever plugin serves them.

| Operation | Method and path |
| --- | --- |
| CreateSpace | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces` |
| GetSpace | `GET /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}` |
| UpdateSpace | `PUT /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}` |
| DeleteSpace | `DELETE /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}` |
| ListSpaces | `GET /_plugins/_memory/spaces` |
| CreateEvent | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events` |
| GetEvent | `GET /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events/{event_id}` |
| BatchGetEvent | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events/_mget` |
| ListEvents | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events/_list` |
| SearchEvents | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events/_search` |
| DeleteEvent | `DELETE /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events/{event_id}` |
| CreateMemory | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories` |
| GetMemory | `GET /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories/{memory_id}` |
| UpdateMemory | `PUT /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories/{memory_id}` |
| DeleteMemory | `DELETE /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories/{memory_id}` |
| ListMemories | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories/_list` |
| SearchMemories | `POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories/_search` |
| Node statistics | `GET /_plugins/_memory/stats` |

Reads are scoped by actor and session:

- ListEvents requires one `actor_id` and one `session_id`.
- SearchEvents and SearchMemories require one `actor_id`, and accept an optional list of `session_ids`.
- ListMemories accepts optional lists of `actor_ids` and `session_ids`.
- GetEvent, BatchGetEvent, and the memory get, update, and delete operations accept the actor, and the session for events, as optional scope checks. A record outside the scope answers as not found.

Request options:

- CreateSpace, CreateEvent, and CreateMemory accept a `client_token`, so a retried write is stored once and the retry returns the stored record.
- CreateEvent accepts `infer: false` to store an event without extracting memories from it.
- List and search operations take `max_results` for the page size, and return a `next_token` for the next page.
- ListEvents and ListMemories take their filters in a request body, sent with `POST` to `_list`.
- CreateEvent and UpdateMemory accept `refresh` (`wait_for` by default, `true`, or `false`). Other writes, except CreateMemory, always wait for the refresh.

### Example

Create a Space with three strategies:

```json
POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces
{
  "name": "support-assistant",
  "memory_strategies": [
    { "type": "SEMANTIC", "name": "facts" },
    { "type": "SUMMARY", "name": "session_summary" },
    {
      "type": "CUSTOM",
      "name": "preferences",
      "configuration": {
        "extraction_prompt": "List the user's stated preferences, one per line.",
        "consolidation_enabled": true
      }
    }
  ],
  "extraction_model_id": "<ML Commons model ID>",
  "embedding_model_id": "<ML Commons model ID>",
  "embedding_dimension": 1024,
  "event_expiry_days": 90,
  "memory_expiry_days": 365
}
```

Write a conversation turn:

```json
POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/events
{
  "actor_id": "user-123",
  "session_id": "session-1",
  "payload": {
    "conversational": {
      "unified": {
        "source": {
          "object": {
            "messages": [
              { "role": "USER", "content": { "text": "I always want a window seat." } },
              { "role": "ASSISTANT", "content": { "text": "Got it. I'll book window seats from now on." } }
            ]
          }
        }
      }
    }
  },
  "metadata": { "channel": "web" }
}
```

The event is stored, the call answers `201 Created`, and memories are extracted in the background. Later, in a new session:

```json
POST /_plugins/_memory/spaces/{space_id}/memories/_search
{
  "actor_id": "user-123",
  "query": { "match": { "memory_text": "seat" } },
  "max_results": 5
}
```

Each result carries `source_event_ids`, so the agent can read the original turns with BatchGetEvent when it needs more detail.

The `conversational.unified.source.object` levels leave room for other payload kinds and sources. Search takes `query` at the top level of the body, as `_search` does. The Space, actor, and session filters are separate fields, so a query cannot widen them.

## Long-term direction: one memory API

We propose that OpenSearch converge on one memory API. This RFC asks only for agreement on the event and memory model as an experimental API. How and when the two APIs converge is decided with the ML Commons maintainers once the new API is stable. Before agentic memory is deprecated, the new API needs to support existing memory workloads, with a compatibility bridge that keeps existing data usable through the new API or a way to move that data into Spaces.

ML Commons agents can use a Space through a memory type. In ML Commons, this is a new memory type next to `AGENTIC_MEMORY`. In a dedicated plugin, ML Commons will add a memory type extension point, which we would contribute; ML Commons still runs without the plugin. Saving to a Space calls no model in the agent's request; extraction runs later in the memory API's own thread pool.

Agent runtimes outside ML Commons can use the new API from the experimental release:

- The [OpenSearch Agent Server](https://github.com/opensearch-project/opensearch-agent-server), for its threads, runs, messages, and events.
- Framework integrations, such as the Strands session manager requested in [.github#443](https://github.com/opensearch-project/.github/issues/443) and the Strands store in [ml-commons#4919](https://github.com/opensearch-project/ml-commons/issues/4919).
- The memory tools in [opensearch-mcp-server-py](https://github.com/opensearch-project/opensearch-mcp-server-py).
- Checkpoint stores for agent frameworks, such as [LangGraph checkpointers](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/concepts/persistence/).

## How it works

This section outlines one implementation. It holds whether the code lives in the ML Commons plugin or in a dedicated plugin.

Diagram 1 shows how an event is stored, how its text is chunked and embedded, how memories are extracted and consolidated, how searches are served, and how records expire. Numbered arrows are the write path, blue arrows are searches, and dashed boxes and arrows run in the background.

<img width="3820" height="2200" alt="Image" src="https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/254636cf-59ec-4b8f-a0e0-3da958810e35" />

*Diagram 1. How the Memory API works on a cluster.*

- **Storage.** Spaces, events, event chunks, and memories live in four system indexes: `.plugins-memory-spaces`, `.plugins-memory-events`, `.plugins-memory-event-chunks`, and `.plugins-memory-memories`. The Job Scheduler jobs live in `.plugins-memory-jobs`. Each event is one document: the full payload, kept as written but not indexed, and a text field with its messages. Each chunk of an event's text is its own document in the chunks index, with the event's ID, Space, actor, session, timestamp, and metadata. Deleting or expiring an event deletes its chunks. Every document stores its Space ID, and its tenant ID when multi-tenancy is on. A get, update, or delete by ID compares the document's Space with the Space in the request and answers 404 on a mismatch, and every search and list filters on the Space. IDs that come from a caller or a model, such as `source_event_ids` or the memories consolidation changes, are checked the same way. Spaces whose embedding models need different vector settings, such as the vector size, use separate chunk and memory indexes. Each index mapping carries a schema version, and older indexes are upgraded in place when a new release adds fields. Application metadata is stored in a `flat_object` field, so the keys an application chooses do not add fields to the shared index mappings.
- **Chunking and embedding.** CreateEvent splits the event's text into chunks by running the Neural Search plugin's `text_chunking` processor through the ingest simulate API, which needs no code dependency on Neural Search, then writes the event and one document per chunk in a single bulk request, so keyword search finds the event at once. Chunk IDs are derived from the event ID, so a retry with the same `client_token` rewrites the same chunks. When a Space names an embedding model, the background work calls it through ML Commons predict and adds a vector to each chunk, so a slow or unavailable model never delays or fails the write. If embedding fails, the Space's backlog job retries it. Event search runs on the chunks index, so each result is one matching chunk with the ID of its event. Extraction embeds each memory before storing it, so consolidation can compare it with stored memories at once. Memories written with CreateMemory get their vector in the background, like chunks. UpdateMemory re-embeds changed content before it returns.
- **Extraction.** Extraction runs on the cluster, in its own bounded thread pool, so there is no second process to deploy. Models are called through ML Commons predict as the implementation's own identity, and only with the model IDs stored on the Space. Whoever sets a Space's models must be allowed to use them. SUMMARY updates one summary per session from the stored summary and the new event, so the summary covers the whole session. Each memory records every event it came from in `source_event_ids`. Consolidation compares a new memory only with memories of the same Space, actor, and strategy, and the model can update or delete only those memories.
- **Extraction under load.** The node that receives an event runs its extraction in the bounded thread pool. Every event stays marked pending until its extraction finishes, so the backlog job retries work lost when a node stops, up to a set number of tries. Each Space has a Job Scheduler job that picks up the Space's pending events on a configurable interval, one minute by default. Job Scheduler runs each job on one of the data nodes that hold a copy of the job's shard, under a lock, so only one node works on a Space's backlog at a time, and the cluster manager node does no extraction. Index State Management, Anomaly Detection, Alerting, and agentic memory's retention job use the same pattern.
- **Search.** Event search and memory search accept only query types whose cost is bounded and that never read other documents: `match`, `match_phrase`, `match_all`, `term`, `terms` (values only), `ids`, `exists`, `bool`, `constant_score`, `boosting`, `range` and `function_score` decay on the time fields, and, when the Space has an embedding model, `neural` and `hybrid`. The implementation checks every clause against that list before the query runs, and rejects anything else with 400. It adds the Space, actor, and session filters itself, inside each `neural` and `hybrid` clause as well as around the query, so a query cannot widen its scope, and a semantic search still finds the closest matches within it. `neural` always uses the Space's embedding model, and `hybrid` scores are combined by a normalization search pipeline that the implementation creates. Both searches can filter by the application's metadata under `metadata.<key>`, and memory search can also filter by `source_event_ids`.
- **Read-after-write.** By default, CreateEvent and UpdateMemory return after the next refresh (`refresh=wait_for`), so a get, list, or keyword search that follows sees the write. CreateMemory answers 202 with the new memory's ID and stores the memory in the background; GetMemory finds it once it is indexed. Semantic search sees a new event once its vectors are added.
- **Expiry.** A Job Scheduler job deletes events older than `event_expiry_days`, with their chunks, and memories older than `memory_expiry_days`. A memory's age counts from when the implementation last wrote it; UpdateMemory does not reset it. An expired memory reads as not found, even before the job deletes it.
- **Running next to the ML Commons memory APIs.** The new API shares no path, index, setting, or permission with the ML Commons memory APIs, so they can run on the same cluster at the same time, and an application can move from one to another at its own pace.

## What is the user experience going to be?

- A cluster administrator turns on the experimental setting, and connects a model through ML Commons.
- A developer creates a Space and starts writing events. Memories are extracted and appear without further calls.
- Optionally, the application writes memories it extracts itself with CreateMemory, using any model or framework it already has, and a single event can skip extraction with `infer: false`.

## Are there any security considerations?

The API relies on the Security plugin for access control. Cluster admins, and the front end that sets the tenant ID, are trusted. OpenSearch users, usually applications, are kept apart per Space. End users do not call the API; their text is untrusted input to the models, and it leaves the cluster for the configured model providers.

- **Permissions.** Each operation is its own transport action, so Security plugin roles can grant operations one by one. Changing a Space's models or prompts, and searching SUMMARY or CUSTOM memories, can reveal event text, so those permissions count as read access to events.
- **Space access.** A Space is private to its owner and to admins (`all_access`) by default. The owner shares it through a `backend_roles` field: a user who holds one of those backend roles can use the Space. Only the owner or an admin can change `backend_roles`, the models, the strategies and prompts, and the expiry settings, and a user who is not an admin can add only backend roles they hold.
- **Records inside a Space.** Access is checked per Space, not per record. A user who can use a Space can read all of its events and memories. Agentic memory, by contrast, limits users who are not admins to the records they wrote. The `actor_id` and `session_id` on a request narrow what it returns, but the application supplies them, so they are not an access check.
- **Tenant isolation.** With multi-tenancy on, the REST layer reads the tenant ID from the `x-tenant-id` header, as ML Commons does, and every Space lookup checks it. The header is trusted as sent, so a deployment must set it from the caller's authenticated identity in a front end, and drop any value the client sends.
- **System indexes.** The memory indexes are system indexes. With the Security plugin, they are closed to users only when `plugins.security.system_indices.enabled` is true, which is off by default, so the implementation warns at startup when it is off. Even then, the super-admin certificate, roles granted `system:admin/system_index`, and snapshot restores can read every Space. Without the Security plugin, there is no access control.
- **Models.** ML Commons connectors hold the model credentials; the memory indexes store none. Event text goes to whatever endpoint a Space's models call, which is why only the owner or an admin can change the models, and the ML Commons setting `plugins.ml_commons.trusted_connector_endpoints_regex` limits where connectors can send it.
- **Model input.** Event text goes into the extraction prompt, and memories are later returned to agents, so text in an event can steer what is stored. Applications need to treat memories as user input. Each event write causes model calls, so a busy writer raises model cost for the whole cluster. ML Commons model rate limits, when set, cap it.

We also propose registering Spaces with the Security plugin's [resource sharing framework](https://docs.opensearch.org/latest/security/access-control/resources/), so an owner can share one Space with specific users, roles, or backend roles. When the framework is on for Spaces, it alone decides who can use a Space; otherwise the backend-role rule above does. The two are never combined.

## Are there any breaking changes to the API and User Experience?

No. The API adds new paths under `/_plugins/_memory`, which exist only when the experimental setting is on. The ML Commons memory APIs, `/_plugins/_ml/memory` and `/_plugins/_ml/memory_containers`, do not change.

## Why should it be built? Any reason not to?

**Why build it:**

- **One memory API for every agent runtime.** Agent state is kept in several places today: agentic memory, the OpenSearch Agent Server's own SQLite store of threads, runs, messages, and events, and each framework adapter. One API lets a memory written by one runtime be read by another.
- **Search over the raw conversation.** Events are indexed for keyword search, and for semantic and hybrid search when a Space names an embedding model, so an agent can find a detail that extraction did not keep.
- **Memories that trace back to their source.** Every memory records the events it came from, whether it was extracted or written with CreateMemory. The link is used to fetch a memory's source events, audit where it came from, and delete what a conversation produced.
- **Safe retries.** A retried write with the same `client_token` is stored once.

**Alternatives we considered:**

- **Change agentic memory to the event and memory model.** Rejected because it breaks agentic memory users, as the section "Why a new API" describes.
- **A client library on top of agentic memory**, as [ml-commons#4919](https://github.com/opensearch-project/ml-commons/issues/4919) and [.github#443](https://github.com/opensearch-project/.github/issues/443) propose for Strands. Rejected because the differences are on the server: the source links, the immutable events, and the actor and session fields. A client library cannot add them.

**Reasons not to:**

- **"I don't think we want to implement memory management twice"** ([ml-commons#1150](https://github.com/opensearch-project/ml-commons/issues/1150)). This is the main cost. OpenSearch would have two memory APIs that extract long-term memories until they converge. The long-term direction proposes converging them on one API, with a compatibility bridge that keeps existing data usable or a way to move it into Spaces.
- **More memory APIs confuse users.** The experimental setting means nobody adopts the new API by accident, and the documentation will say which API fits which need until agentic memory is deprecated.
- **Agentic memory has more features today.** The new API starts with a focused set, and features can be added based on community interest.

## What will it take to execute?

- **Dependencies.** The ML Commons plugin for model calls, the Job Scheduler plugin for the extraction backlog and expiry, the Neural Search plugin for chunking and for `neural` and `hybrid` queries, the k-NN plugin for vector fields, and optionally the Security plugin.
- **Versions.** The API runs its background work under its own plugin identity, which needs the Security plugin fix that lets a plugin identity use its own system indexes ([security#5858](https://github.com/opensearch-project/security/pull/5858), in 3.5). If the code lives in ML Commons, ML Commons first adopts plugin identity.
- **Clients.** The API is added to opensearch-api-specification after it is implemented, so clients can be generated from it.
- **Cost.** Each event leads to model calls for each strategy: one to extract, one to consolidate when consolidation is on, and embedding calls when the Space has an embedding model. The implementation can batch these calls, such as several turns of a session in one extraction call, without changing the API.
- **Process.** This RFC, open for community review. If the community chooses a dedicated plugin, a repository request and the project's security review for a new repository follow.

## Any remaining open questions?

We would like the community's view on these questions:

1. **Where should the code live?** The API design is the same either way.

   - *In the ML Commons plugin*, next to the existing memory APIs. No new repository, release pipeline, or set of maintainers. Changes are reviewed in the existing ML Commons community and its weekly meeting, where backward compatibility is already checked. Other plugins already call ML Commons through a small client layer.
   - *In a dedicated plugin* that calls ML Commons for models, as the Neural Search and Flow Framework plugins do. Memory gets its own owners and an optional install, and ML Commons stays focused on models and inference, a split proposed for memory in 2023 ([ml-commons#1150](https://github.com/opensearch-project/ml-commons/issues/1150#issuecomment-1666021113)) and for agents in [.github#398](https://github.com/opensearch-project/.github/issues/398). The cost is another repository to build, release, and secure.
   - *Paths.* We propose `/_plugins/_memory` in both cases, so the answer does not change the API. If the community prefers ML Commons' own prefix when the code lives there, the same operations would sit under it, for example `/_plugins/_ml/spaces/{space_id}/events`. `/_plugins/_ml/memory` is taken by conversation memory.
2. **Agentic memory.** What should the path to one API look like, and would ML Commons add the memory type extension point described in "Long-term direction"? The existing `REMOTE_AGENTIC_MEMORY` memory type calls fixed agentic memory paths ([ml-commons#4572](https://github.com/opensearch-project/ml-commons/issues/4572)), so it cannot reach a Space as it stands.
3. **Leaving experimental status.** What should the API show before it becomes stable: a number of releases without breaking changes, use by ML Commons agents, or a benchmark of extraction quality?

Out of scope for this RFC: OpenSearch Dashboards support and framework adapters (LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Strands). With a dedicated plugin, the memory type extension point would be its own ML Commons change.

items.title: [Campaign] State-of-the-art NeqSim MCP process simulation and troubleshooting
items.body:
## Goal

Make the NeqSim MCP server a state-of-the-art, governed oil-and-gas process-engineering tool that can:

- translate a short engineering request, equipment list, facility narrative, structured data, or supported PFD/P&ID/DEXPI description into a reviewable NeqSim simulation;
- grow the same canonical model from one calculation or unit operation into a large, multi-area facility with recycles, controls, constraints, and reusable model state;
- execute the calculations routinely needed by process, flow-assurance, production-technology, operating-support, and troubleshooting engineers;
- investigate operational symptoms through explicit hypotheses, simulations, sensitivity cases, and evidence rather than unsupported diagnosis;
- return concise operator-facing conclusions while retaining detailed balances, assumptions, provenance, convergence evidence, validation findings, and selectively retrievable large-model results.

The server is an advisory engineering calculation layer. It must not autonomously control a plant, write to operational systems, claim accountable engineering approval, or hide missing data and model limitations.

## Current baseline to reuse

Do not rebuild capabilities already present on current `master`.

- The `neqsim-mcp-server` module already provides governed profiles, standard response envelopes, validation, benchmark-trust metadata, traceability, STDIO/HTTP transports, schemas, resources, and guided prompts.
- `runFlash`, `runProcess`, `manageModel`, `runPipeline`, `runOperationalStudy`, lifecycle/session tools, and domain runners provide an extensive curated surface.
- Merged PR #2874 established caller identity and recoverable security enforcement.
- Merged PR #2875 established model handles, solved-model reuse, bounded execution, response-size control, large-process evidence, catalog coverage checks, and stronger benchmark contracts.
- Merged PR #3152 added runtime capability inspection/execution, canonical replayable process definitions, multi-area and equipment-design preservation, compressor anti-surge topology, capacity/bottleneck evidence, and typed detailed two-fluid pipeline results.
- Coordinate process/P&ID/DEXPI ingestion with #2899, dynamic studies with #2911, flash/stability work with #2937, and the merged production-optimization foundation recorded in #2941. Do not duplicate or compete with those roadmaps.

## Engineering and product principles

1. **One canonical model.** Use normal NeqSim fluids, streams, `ProcessSystem`, `ProcessModel`, topology, design, and result objects. Do not create a second incompatible MCP-only simulator.
2. **Progressive construction.** A one-off PVT or equipment calculation must be reusable as an input to a stream, process area, facility, study, and report.
3. **Explicit units and bases.** Distinguish standard/actual, mass/molar/volume flow, absolute/gauge pressure, wet/dry basis, and operating/design conditions.
4. **No silent invention.** Facility parsing must return mapped facts, assumptions, ambiguities, missing data, unsupported items, and questions. Inferred values require provenance and confidence.
5. **Evidence before diagnosis.** Troubleshooting must separate observations, hypotheses, model tests, findings, uncertainty, and recommended next measurements/actions.
6. **Fail visibly.** Non-convergence, extrapolation, inconsistent measurements, unit errors, ambiguous topology, invalid thermodynamic choices, or unavailable validation evidence must produce structured diagnostics.
7. **Bounded operation.** Preserve time, memory, concurrency, payload, and security limits; make cancellation and partial-result behavior explicit.
8. **Layered results.** Return an operator-sized summary first and permit deterministic retrieval of area, equipment, stream, profile, balance, diagnostic, and provenance detail.
9. **Validation maturity is explicit.** Runtime availability is not proof of engineering validation. Every result must carry model choice, applicability, benchmark status, and limitations.
10. **Backward compatibility.** Evolve stable contracts deliberately, with schemas, migration guidance, and contract tests.

## Roadmap

### Phase 0 — Current-master audit and acceptance matrix

- [ ] Inventory every MCP tool, resource, prompt, schema, runner, supported equipment type, report path, deployment profile, test, guide, and known limitation on current `master`.
- [ ] Reconcile open/merged/closed MCP work and prove what #2874, #2875, and #3152 deliver on current `master`.
- [ ] Establish public synthetic acceptance fixtures at four scales: a single calculation/unit, a small train, a multi-area facility, and a large facility with recycles.
- [ ] Create a traceability matrix from each campaign criterion to source, tests, documentation, benchmark evidence, or a confirmed gap.
- [ ] Record baseline runtime, memory, response size, tool-call count, convergence, balance closure, and report usefulness.
- [ ] Define a machine-readable capability/maturity matrix by engineering discipline.

### Phase 1 — Facility description to reviewable simulation

- [ ] Define a versioned facility-description contract accepting narrative facts, equipment/stream tables, structured JSON, and supported diagram/DEXPI references without mixing extracted facts with inference.
- [ ] Produce a deterministic normalized specification containing areas, fluids, streams, equipment, connections, operating/design cases, controls, constraints, data provenance, units, confidence, gaps, and questions.
- [ ] Add component/equipment/tag synonym resolution with explicit ambiguity diagnostics.
- [ ] Validate topology, port/phase compatibility, unit consistency, component coverage, boundary conditions, recycle closure, required equipment data, and thermodynamic-model suitability before solving.
- [ ] Generate a canonical `ProcessSystem` or multi-area `ProcessModel` plus editable/replayable process definition.
- [ ] Support incremental refinement: add an area, stream, equipment item, case, control, or constraint without rebuilding unrelated solved state.
- [ ] Coordinate diagram ingestion and round-trip semantics with #2899 rather than implementing a parallel P&ID model.
- [ ] Require an explicit review checkpoint before inferred facility content is treated as an accepted simulation input.

### Phase 2 — Small-to-large composable process construction

- [ ] Provide reusable templates/builders for common oil-and-gas building blocks: well/feed, inlet separation, compression, dehydration, gas treatment, NGL recovery, stabilization, produced-water handling, export, injection, utilities, relief/blowdown/flare, and tie-in facilities.
- [ ] Preserve live stream identity, multi-port topology, area boundaries, recycles, adjusters, controllers, design constraints, equipment charts, geometry, and model revisions.
- [ ] Add predictable model composition, cloning, revision, comparison, serialization, Python replay, and selective re-solve behavior.
- [ ] Make unsupported equipment/connections explicit and extensible through reviewed adapters.
- [ ] Prove deterministic build and execution for small, medium, and large multi-area cases.

### Phase 3 — Process-engineering calculation coverage

- [ ] **Fluids/PVT:** fluid characterization, plus fractions, EOS/mixing-rule selection, TP/PH/PS/TV flashes, phase envelopes, dew/bubble points, density/viscosity/thermal properties, standard volumes, calorific value/Wobbe, PVT experiments and regression where validated.
- [ ] **Flow assurance:** hydrate, water/MEG/TEG, wax, asphaltene, corrosion/scale screening, single- and multiphase pipe/well calculations, profiles, cooldown/transients, erosion and operating envelopes with applicability boundaries.
- [ ] **Core equipment:** streams, mixers/splitters, separators/scrubbers, valves/chokes, compressors/expanders, pumps, heaters/coolers/heat exchangers, columns/absorbers/strippers, tanks, pipelines/wells, reactors, utilities, and relevant mechanical/design calculations.
- [ ] **Facility studies:** mass/energy/component balances, equipment performance, capacity/utilization, bottlenecks, operating envelopes, turndown, recycle/control behavior, production allocation/optimization handoff, emissions/energy KPIs, and case comparison.
- [ ] Route eligible generic static calculations through runtime capability discovery only when the exact signature, bounds, maturity, and response contract are known; keep stateful calculations behind curated runners.

### Phase 4 — Troubleshooting and operating-support workflow

- [ ] Define a structured troubleshooting case: symptom, time/operating context, observed values, expected behavior, data quality, relevant equipment/topology, hypotheses, tests, findings, confidence, and actions.
- [ ] Convert operator/support-engineer descriptions into testable hypotheses without claiming causality from correlation.
- [ ] Add reusable diagnostic patterns for separation loss, compressor underperformance/surge/recycle, valve restriction, exchanger fouling, column off-spec, hydrate/condensation risk, pipeline pressure loss, recycle non-convergence, instrument inconsistency, and changing feed composition.
- [ ] Compare current/reference/what-if states with conservation, thermodynamic consistency, equipment limits, nearby operating points, and sensitivity/uncertainty evidence.
- [ ] Distinguish process-model mismatch, bad/missing data, equipment degradation, control behavior, and numerical failure.
- [ ] Recommend the next safest measurement, check, or simulation; never issue plant-control commands.
- [ ] Build a public synthetic fault library with known injected causes and measurable pass/fail diagnostic criteria.

### Phase 5 — Dynamic, operability, and scenario studies

- [ ] Support bounded steady-state, quasi-steady, and dynamic study orchestration with explicit solver/model selection.
- [ ] Compose startup/shutdown, trip, control-response, depressurization, cooldown, compressor recycle, slugging, and constraint-change cases where the underlying NeqSim model is validated.
- [ ] Coordinate underlying dynamic-model implementation with #2911 and pipeline/flash campaigns rather than duplicating solver work.
- [ ] Preserve initial state, case definitions, time series, convergence, event chronology, safeguards, limitations, and reproducible replay.
- [ ] Keep all outputs advisory and clearly separate screening from qualified dynamic studies.

### Phase 6 — Large-process execution and lifecycle

- [ ] Benchmark representative small (3–5 unit), medium (25–50 unit), large (150+ unit), and stress-scale facility models where feasible.
- [ ] Improve registration, revision, dependency-aware partial solving, warm-state reuse, caching, immutable snapshots, concurrency isolation, cancellation, timeout, recovery, and deterministic replay.
- [ ] Prevent repeated full solves for read-only result retrieval.
- [ ] Stream or page large results by model → area → equipment/stream → property/profile instead of producing context-breaking payloads.
- [ ] Preserve the standard compact response envelope and deterministic selective retrieval after truncation.
- [ ] Record runtime/memory/payload baselines and conservative regression thresholds by environment; do not hide degraded accuracy or convergence to meet a performance target.
- [ ] Add multi-client and tenant-isolation tests for mutable models and long-running studies.

### Phase 7 — Engineering results and reporting

- [ ] Define typed, versioned result contracts for fluids, equipment, streams, areas, complete facilities, scenarios, troubleshooting findings, and comparisons.
- [ ] Provide summary/detail levels that retain exact units, basis, case, timestamp/revision, model/provenance, convergence, validation, warnings, and engineering-review requirements.
- [ ] Generate concise operator and support-engineer summaries: what changed, likely mechanisms, evidence, uncertainty, limits, and recommended next action.
- [ ] Generate process-engineering results: stream tables, equipment duties/performance, mass/component/energy balances, constraints/utilization, profiles, case deltas, diagnostics, and assumptions.
- [ ] Support deterministic Markdown/JSON/CSV and suitable visual/report artifacts without making downloadable files the only place results can be reviewed.
- [ ] Validate report completeness, numerical consistency, units, ordering, clipping/size, and selective-detail links for large facilities.

### Phase 8 — MCP usability, schemas, and agent cooperation

- [ ] Make discovery task-oriented: “build this facility,” “run this calculation,” “explain this symptom,” and “compare these cases,” not only tool-name discovery.
- [ ] Keep input/output schemas complete, bounded, example-backed, and synchronized with the actual tool surface.
- [ ] Provide fix-oriented validation errors with field paths, accepted units/enums, alternatives, and recoverable next steps.
- [ ] Support resumable multi-step studies and explicit handoffs between facility parsing, model construction, simulation, troubleshooting, validation, and reporting.
- [ ] Add end-to-end protocol tests over STDIO and Streamable HTTP using real MCP clients or a standards-conforming harness.
- [ ] Keep NeqSim agents/skills and MCP contracts synchronized; route domain gaps to the underlying NeqSim capability instead of papering them over in prompts.

### Phase 9 — Trust, security, deployment, and observability

- [ ] Preserve profile enforcement, identity, tenant isolation, audit, approval gates, response/execution bounds, OIDC/HTTP security, and advisory-only digital-twin behavior.
- [ ] Add calculation/model/revision correlation IDs, structured timings, cache/solve provenance, and privacy-safe diagnostics.
- [ ] Test malformed, adversarial, oversized, recursive, unsupported, and resource-exhausting inputs.
- [ ] Maintain deployment recipes and health/readiness evidence for desktop, CI, container, and governed team/enterprise use.
- [ ] Prove that secrets, credentials, proprietary input data, and raw plant data are not leaked through logs, reports, caches, or cross-tenant handles.

### Phase 10 — Executed reference workflows and completion gate

- [ ] Execute and retain outputs for at least: one PVT/flash study, one equipment calculation, one small facility, one large multi-area facility, and several known-cause troubleshooting cases.
- [ ] Demonstrate narrative facility description → normalized specification/gap review → canonical model → execution → validation → operator summary → detailed engineering report → model revision/replay.
- [ ] Demonstrate progressive reuse from a single fluid/equipment calculation into a complete facility.
- [ ] Validate key engineering results against analytical checks, published/public benchmarks, independent models, experimental data, or defensible physical bounds.
- [ ] Complete focused and proportionate broader tests, formatting/static-analysis/documentation gates, exact protocol tests, security tests, and rendered artifact inspection.
- [ ] Publish a final capability/maturity/benchmark/limitation matrix with exact evidence links.
- [ ] Perform an independent current-`master` audit: no unmet definition-of-done criterion, no active campaign PR, no unresolved critical/high defect, no stale documentation/schema/example claim.

## Definition of done

This campaign is complete only when current default-branch evidence demonstrates all of the following:

- A user can start with a typical oil-and-gas engineering question or facility narrative and obtain a reviewable canonical model with explicit mappings, assumptions, gaps, and questions.
- The same model can be extended from a single calculation/unit into a multi-area large facility without incompatible representations.
- Representative PVT, flash, valve, compressor, separator, exchanger, column, pump, pipeline/well, flow-assurance, balance, performance, capacity, and scenario studies execute through documented contracts where NeqSim has validated functionality.
- Known-cause synthetic troubleshooting cases produce evidence-backed, uncertainty-aware findings and useful next actions without unsafe control advice.
- Small, medium, and 150+ unit acceptance models are reproducible, bounded, isolated across clients, and usable without repeated unnecessary full solves or oversized responses.
- Operator summaries and detailed engineering results are consistent, unit-complete, selectively retrievable, reproducible, and explicit about convergence, validation maturity, assumptions, and limitations.
- Every public tool/resource/prompt/schema is covered by contract tests and current documentation; security, governance, execution, compatibility, and documentation gates pass.
- The MCP server remains an advisory calculation and decision-support tool; it never claims plant authority or accountable engineering approval.

## Campaign coordination and run ledger

- Maintain at most **one active implementation PR for this MCP campaign** and no more than **ten open autonomous NeqSim implementation PRs overall**.
- Before every run, read this issue and newest comments, current `master`, repository instructions, current MCP source/docs/tests, related open/recent PRs, reviews/checks, and overlap roadmaps.
- Search for merged or active functionality before selecting work. Reuse it and never create a competing implementation.
- Select the largest coherent dependency-ready increment that remains one reviewable concept. Include implementation, tests, validation, documentation, schemas/examples, and agent/skill contract updates when coupled.
- Never write to `master`, merge, enable auto-merge, force-push, or mark a draft ready for review.
- Every productive run must append a ledger comment containing: timestamp; exact base/head; active autonomous PR count; selected roadmap item and stop boundary; files/PR; tests and engineering validation; documentation impact; limitations/blocker; and next dependency.
- Open or draft PR work remains in progress until merged. Mark roadmap boxes complete only from verified merged default-branch evidence.
- Notify only for a new/materially updated PR, a changed blocker/decision, first `READY TO MERGE` classification for an exact head, or final campaign completion. Keep no-op runs silent.


## User-directed full agent/MCP exposure follow-up (2026-10-04)

[Draft #4201](https://github.com/equinor/neqsim/pull/4201) implements the first coverage increment requested alongside #4191. It is user-directed work, separate from the autonomous test-layout PR #4194. Preserve the coverage protocol assertions across #4194's harness relocation. Do not treat draft work as completed default-branch evidence.

The implementation roadmap and explicit exit gates live in `docs/development/ENGINEERING_CAPABILITY_COVERAGE.md` on #4201.

- [ ] **Baseline:** merge and verify the source-derived catalog, API → skill → agent → MCP route → test-source mappings, paginated discovery and freshness CI. Draft #4201 inventories 3,339 public primary Java types after #4191, with 12 seed workflows / 18 anchors; 3,241 types require classification/mapping review. These are source counts, not unsupported-operation counts.
- [ ] **Operation contracts:** classify supported, internal, experimental and deprecated operations; bind supported signatures, units, applicability, setup, schemas and examples to existing execution routes.
- [ ] **Stateful lifecycle:** qualify construction, mutation, cloning, revision, serialization/replay, property access and connections through canonical model runners.
- [ ] **Domain completion:** deliver cohesive adapters + contracts + skills + examples + positive/invalid-input execution fixtures, in order: thermodynamics/PVT; equipment/facilities; chemistry/flow assurance; wells/pipelines/networks; dynamics/control/optimization; engineering studies.
- [ ] **Engineering qualification:** reconcile existing benchmark evidence and add independent expected values, tolerances, units, conservation/convergence/constraint checks, nearby cases and exact-build receipts; exercise actual MCP workflows from calculation through multi-area facility and reporting.
- [ ] **Release enforcement:** gate API/schema drift, numerical validity, transport, cancellation, response size and compatibility; independently audit completion on default branch.

**Completion rule:** 100% of classified supported engineering operations must have agent discovery and a documented MCP execution route, plus successful and invalid-input fixtures. Engineering qualification is a separate, evidence-backed status. Unknown classifications or missing required routes keep completion false. Source mentions and test-file presence never imply successful execution.

Initial validation on #4201: 48 focused Java tests, 51 Python tests after #4191 integration, plus packaged STDIO capability checks; exact final-head validation is recorded in the PR. Full Java suite, HTTP transport and independent qualification are separate gates.

milestone.title: SaaS Platform Foundation
milestone.description: Controlled SaaS integration for the existing AI observability platform: organization ownership, trusted identity, platform/tenant RBAC, lifecycle administration, licensing, audit, security and production evidence. Planning only; existing baseline issues retain ownership. Tests run locally or owner-run, never in GitHub Actions.

items.body:
Planning backlog only. Created after repository/backlog review on 2026-09-21. Unchecked criteria describe future delivery; this issue is not an implementation, test result or production approval.

## Objective

Integrate the new SaaS principal, lifecycle and ownership rules into existing business modules without rewriting them.

## Background

#5 already owns cross-store tenant enforcement, and many domain models/tests already use organization_id and negative tenant cases. #62/#63/#77 own workflow, artifact and retention foundations. This issue owns the SaaS-specific module rollout and legacy-data reconciliation, not rebuilding isolation or assuming current tests prove production coverage.

## Scope

Module-by-module SaaS context/state integration, approved ownership migration and regression verification; license integration only where a feature is explicitly license-controlled.

## Detailed Requirements

- Complete the architecture ownership inventory for projects/apps/environments, telemetry/traces/logs/metrics, LLM/agent/RAG records, sessions, evals/datasets/experiments, prompts, budgets/pricing, integrations, alerts/notifications, workforce/archive/access, ledger/finance, supervision/cases, views/reports and configuration.
- For each entity declare PLATFORM-SCOPED, ORGANIZATION-SCOPED, USER-SCOPED or GLOBAL. Preserve valid global catalogs and user-owned saved views with tenant constraints; trace end-user IDs and workforce subjects are not portal users. Direct organization_id is required only where justified; parent-derived ownership must remain provable.
- Extend repositories/services/APIs/queries and frontend data access to use authoritative single-org identity, resource ownership and organization status. Platform cross-org operations stay behind the distinct permission boundary, not generalized unscoped queries.
- Where missing, add reviewed org ownership columns, tenant-safe/composite foreign keys and indexes with expand/backfill/validate/contract migrations. Preserve IDs and history; quarantine ambiguous ownership, reconcile counts/hashes and prove rollback/restart recovery instead of mapping unknown rows to one organization.
- Reuse #5 PostgreSQL RLS/FORCE RLS and non-bypass app role, trusted ClickHouse query templates, server-derived VictoriaMetrics routes, tenant-bound S3 manifests/links and explicit Kafka/outbox/Temporal context. Propagate status/revocation checks through queues, async/thread bridges, exports, retries, cache keys and restore paths.
- Update shared client/filter/query-cache contracts so ordinary users cannot switch organization by changing URL/header/body or cached selector. Cancel incompatible requests and clear stale data after authority changes; enforce API checks independently.
- Require License Enforcement only for the modules/operations explicitly listed in the entitlement matrix. Non-license-controlled tenant integration proceeds in parallel; do not make later full administration UI or unrelated domain rewrites prerequisite to early data ownership.
- Preserve #95 purpose-limited content access, legal holds and #77 deletion/recovery semantics. Organization shutdown must not destroy retained evidence or grant broad platform data access.

## Dependencies

- [[SAAS] Implement Multi-Tenant Organization Foundation](https://github.com/rameshsraj/ai-observability-platform/issues/170) (#170)
- [[SAAS] Implement SaaS-Aware Authentication Foundation](https://github.com/rameshsraj/ai-observability-platform/issues/171) (#171)
- [[SAAS] Implement RBAC and Permission Framework](https://github.com/rameshsraj/ai-observability-platform/issues/172) (#172)
- [[SAAS] Implement Organization Lifecycle Management](https://github.com/rameshsraj/ai-observability-platform/issues/174) (#174)
- [[SAAS] Implement Organization Admin Management](https://github.com/rameshsraj/ai-observability-platform/issues/175) (#175)
- [[SAAS] Implement Organization User Management](https://github.com/rameshsraj/ai-observability-platform/issues/176) (#176)
- Conditional: [[SAAS] Implement License Enforcement and Usage Limits](https://github.com/rameshsraj/ai-observability-platform/issues/178) (#178) - required only for explicitly license-controlled modules/features; nonlicensed tenant integration is not blocked.

Existing prerequisite contracts/deliveries (consume their evidence; do not reimplement):
- #5 - Implement tenant isolation middleware and data access enforcement

## Blocks

- [[SAAS] Implement Platform and Organization Dashboards](https://github.com/rameshsraj/ai-observability-platform/issues/180) (#180)
- [[SAAS] Perform SaaS Security Hardening and Authorization Testing](https://github.com/rameshsraj/ai-observability-platform/issues/182) (#182)
- [[SAAS] Complete SaaS Integration and Production Readiness](https://github.com/rameshsraj/ai-observability-platform/issues/183) (#183)

## Related Existing Issues

- #2 - Implement organization, project, application, and environment domain model and schema
- #3 - Implement authentication service: API keys, OIDC SSO, and service accounts
- #4 - Implement RBAC with roles, permissions, and resource-level access control
- #5 - Implement tenant isolation middleware and data access enforcement
- #7 - Implement OTLP/gRPC and HTTP trace ingestion endpoints
- #9 - Implement trace store schema and query layer in ClickHouse
- #10 - Implement metrics aggregation pipeline and time-series store
- #11 - Implement log ingestion and correlation with traces
- #36 - Implement dataset model, versioning, import/export, and trace-derived items
- #43 - Implement cost calculation engine and model pricing map
- #54 - Implement global filters, saved views, and drill-down navigation
- #62 - Implement durable evaluation orchestration with Temporal and idempotent result commits
- #63 - Implement tenant-scoped S3 artifact storage, retention, deletion and recovery
- #76 - Implement tenant-scoped security and administrative audit trail
- #77 - Implement cross-store retention, deletion and restore reconciliation
- #82 - Implement core integration contracts and secure connection lifecycle
- #87 - Implement workforce identity, directory sync and historical cost-center attribution
- #94 - Build auditable employee prompt and conversation archive with integrity and legal holds
- #95 - Enforce supervisor scope, purpose-limited prompt access and content-read auditing
- #96 - Implement authoritative AI usage ledger with token provenance and workforce attribution
- #97 - Reconcile AI invoices, subscriptions and credits with finance audit reports
- #100 - Build enterprise prompt usage and Intelligent Supervisor dashboard with audit drill-downs

## Implementation Tasks

- [ ] Publish an entity/module coverage matrix with baseline issue owner, actual enforcement path, migration delta and test evidence.
- [ ] Implement only uncovered SaaS integration/migration changes, using shared policy and store adapters.
- [ ] Reconcile legacy data and regression-check each affected API/UI/worker path before phased rollout.

## Security Considerations

- Test ownership before reads/counts/exports and writes; IDOR/BOLA and shared-cache leaks apply to all modules, not only administration.
- Absent context, stale permission, forged resource IDs and privileged database-role bypass must fail closed; employee content restrictions remain stricter than tenant membership.

## Testing Requirements

- Two-tenant/two-project tests must attempt foreign detail/list/search/count/update/delete/bulk/export/job/object/metric access, including reused connections after exceptions and async/thread transitions.
- Test fresh/legacy migration, concurrent writes during backfill, restart/replay, quarantine/reconciliation, legal holds and restore. Reuse existing negative tests and add uncovered SaaS regressions.
- Run real supported adapter integration profiles; SQLite or HTML fixtures alone cannot prove PostgreSQL RLS or cross-store production isolation.

Repository policy: all pytest, Vitest, Playwright, integration, security, visual and qualification tests run locally or in owner-run environments; attach evidence to PRs/issues. All lint, typecheck and builds also run in owner-run environments; no GitHub Actions. No tests are executed by this planning task.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Every identified business entity has justified ownership and a traced SaaS integration/test path; no blind global schema change.
- [ ] Organization A users cannot access Organization B resources, counts, artifacts or queued results through any supported module.
- [ ] Existing functionality remains supported and legacy records have deterministic migrated ownership or explicit quarantine with remediation.
- [ ] Licensed modules include the enforcement prerequisite; nonlicensed module integration has no artificial licensing or UI dependency.

## Deliverables

- Ownership/module evidence matrix, reviewed incremental integrations/migrations, reconciliation/rollback report and cross-store regression results.

Delivery workflow: implement in dependency order on a branch, review/merge the PR, then keep the issue open and mark PENDING VERIFICATION with evidence and the existing Project status. Do not close issues. Existing source changes and existing issue ownership must be preserved.

## Out of Scope

- Whole-application rewrite, reimplementing #5/#62/#63/#77, new storage products, blanket tenant columns and blanket licensing of every feature.

# Phase26 — Support Hub & Conversation Management

**Implementation-ready specification. All D1–D40 decisions and amendments are ratified; the founder confirmed the testing approach.**

Support Hub is one cohesive Asym surface with shared native CRM context and correctly authorized owner actions. This specification preserves the complete email/intake/work lifecycle, private collaboration, drafts and reading preferences, contextual guidance, safe file reading and recoverable Unwanted/future-mail holding journeys.

**Start with the user-story book**, then follow its stable US26/REQ26/AC26 identifiers into the detailed requirement volumes. The glossary fixes domain language; OpenSpec carries observable behavior, design and the unchecked implementation/qualification checklist. The source trace records every captured section's authority and disposition.

The full package contains **217 independently verifiable user stories, 2,210 detailed requirement definitions, 717 main OpenSpec scenarios, and all additional exact proof/operating-control suites**. It covers **all 40 ratified decisions**, including D27-C, D29-X01 and every accepted correction. Numerical limits, state/audience/source rules, failure recovery and release gates remain binding.

**Email Studio/P17** owns governed reusable content, canonical authoring and whole-message preparation. **P6** owns actual communication, provider evidence and recovery. **Support** owns human work, source-specific intent and private drafting; canonical intake owns receiving and held-mail decisions. CRM and giving/care domains retain their own truth, permissions and mutations. These seams are specified throughout the requirements, not left as integration assumptions.

**Confirmed proof approach:** real authenticated Support/API and canonical intake/job boundaries on disposable local Supabase; focused actual database permission/concurrency/migration proof; and full Playwright journeys on that same backend. Existing frameworks are reused and real-provider qualification stays separate.

No feature implementation or implementation-ticket graph is included. Specification/documentary validation has passed; product runtime, provider, accessibility, intended-user and release evidence remains required before activation. Local formal/OpenSpec mirrors are validated; this publication is the complete issue-tracker specification and does not claim a source PR.

items.body:
Consolidation package from the review-debt compare (NATHAN-CONSOLIDATE, OA-ConsolCompare, pinned main 81b71101). Plan: `polish/consolidate/compare/packages.md`; per-row verdicts and evidence: `compare/claims.tsv`.

The hosted function waits on recovery with no bound and on one connection, so one stalled query stops every request (#1411). #1368 handed the recovery rebuild to #1395. Same area: worker proposal identity, trace read budget, local agent security minors.

items.body:
![Find your focus and passion across seven vLLM Semantic Router Workgroups](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vllm-project/semantic-router/main/website/static/img/blog/vllm/2026-08-24-workgroups-invitation/workgroups-invitation-hero.png)

## Find Your Focus and Passion

vLLM Semantic Router organizes its durable open-source technical directions
into seven Workgroups. A Workgroup gives contributors a clear place to find
people with the same interests, shape accepted Epics, build together, and grow
with the community.

> A Workgroup is a technical home, not a repository permission level.

- [Explore the Workgroups](https://vllm-sr.ai/community/work-groups)
- [Read the community invitation](https://vllm-sr.ai/blog/join-vllm-sr-workgroups)

## Seven Workgroups

| Direction | What it owns |
| --- | --- |
| [MoM & Routing](https://github.com/vllm-project/semantic-router/issues/2965) | Model pools, versioned routing recipes, multi-model collaboration, and the recipe lifecycle |
| [Router Models & Inference Runtime](https://github.com/vllm-project/semantic-router/issues/2966) | Router Model improvement and new model families, typed signals, and an extensible inference runtime |
| [Data Plane & Networking](https://github.com/vllm-project/semantic-router/issues/2967) | Standalone and gateway-integrated request paths, streaming, reliability, and performance |
| [Enterprise & Environment](https://github.com/vllm-project/semantic-router/issues/2968) | Management security and audit, configuration lifecycle, observability, capacity planning, reference deployments, and supported environments and hardware |
| [Agentic & Context](https://github.com/vllm-project/semantic-router/issues/2987) | Context optimization, memory and session boundaries, and safe model or workflow switching for long-running agents |
| [Developer Experience & Ecosystem](https://github.com/vllm-project/semantic-router/issues/2970) | CLI, Dashboard, documentation, agent skills, integrations, tutorials, and contributor experience |
| [Evaluation & Quality](https://github.com/vllm-project/semantic-router/issues/2969) | Shared evaluation contracts, benchmarks, published results, and regression gates |

The planning hierarchy is:

`Mission → Direction → Workgroup → bounded Epic → accepted issue`

## How Workgroup participation works

Joining a Workgroup as a Member follows four steps:

1. **Apply** — choose a Workgroup above, open its charter, and leave a first-person application comment with your background and interests.
2. **Claim** — choose an available issue from your Workgroup's comment on the [current Workgroup Issues ledger](https://github.com/vllm-project/semantic-router/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3Acommunity+label%3Aaccepted+label%3Aowner%2Fmaintainers+%22Workgroup+Issues%22+in%3Atitle), open the target issue, and comment `/assign`. The claim counts only after your name appears in the target issue Assignees field.
3. **Deliver** — open a focused PR linked to the claimed issue and get a substantive contribution merged.
4. **Join** — eligible contributors are added through one reviewed roster PR. Membership becomes canonical after that PR merges.

### If you have not applied

Choose a Workgroup, open its charter from the table, and submit a Member application. You can then claim an available issue from your Workgroup's comment on the [current Workgroup Issues ledger](https://github.com/vllm-project/semantic-router/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3Acommunity+label%3Aaccepted+label%3Aowner%2Fmaintainers+%22Workgroup+Issues%22+in%3Atitle).

### If you have applied but do not know how to start

Choose an available issue from your Workgroup's weekly comment and use `/assign` on the target issue. If none fits, comment `Need task: wg/<slug>` on the [current Workgroup Issues ledger](https://github.com/vllm-project/semantic-router/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3Acommunity+label%3Aaccepted+label%3Aowner%2Fmaintainers+%22Workgroup+Issues%22+in%3Atitle) so the next review can prepare options; this does not assign a task automatically.

### If you already joined

Choose an available issue from your Workgroup's weekly comment. Use `/assign` on the target issue, or leave `Need task: wg/<slug>` on the [current Workgroup Issues ledger](https://github.com/vllm-project/semantic-router/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3Acommunity+label%3Aaccepted+label%3Aowner%2Fmaintainers+%22Workgroup+Issues%22+in%3Atitle) when the current list has no suitable work.

A contribution qualifies a contributor for the Workgroup that owns that work. A requested Lead role follows the same contribution path but requires a separate human role decision.

For the complete role guidance and card examples, read [How to join and work together](https://vllm-sr.ai/blog/join-vllm-sr-workgroups).

Find your focus and passion. Build with the community. Grow together.

items.title: Phase 5: shared-pool pressure response (reconciliation-triggered eviction scoped to the co-location group)
items.body:
Part of **Phase 5 — kvcached oversubscription & co-location policy** (spec: `docs/project/overall-plan.md:385-398`; plan: `.omp/plans/phase5-plan.md`, review-clean after two adversarial rounds).

## Summary
When a device's kvcached pool is under pressure (used ≈ pool total), the control plane's reconciliation tick reclaims capacity through the eviction engine, scoped to the pressure device's co-location group — the first memory-pressure eviction trigger in the system (eviction is demand-only today).

## Ground truth (verified against code)
- No memory-pressure/idle/background eviction trigger exists (`grep idle|autoSleep|sleepAfter|inactivity control-plane/src`: nothing); the two existing triggers are deploy-fail (`models.ts:472-514`) and wake-shortfall (`models.ts:1814-1878`).
- Hook point: `ReconciliationService.tick` → `safeStep('refreshMemoryBudgets')` (`reconciliation.ts:164`); `DeviceBudget.kvCache` is validated + attached every tick (`memory-budget.ts:83-113, :269-270`).
- Victim selection: `EvictionEngine.selectVictims` (`eviction.ts:62-117`), LRU by per-model `lastInferenceAt`, candidates ACTIVE|SLEEPING unpinned, sized by configured `requiredMemory`; `EvictionStrategy` is the pluggable seam (`eviction.ts:16-18`). `EvictionCandidate` has no `deviceIndex` — device scoping must not re-derive the co-location group (#276 owns the helper).
- vLLM sleep = weights→host RAM (L1); a slept co-tenant's kvcached pool segment persists (`kvcached_pools.py`), so pool stats keep flowing after sleep — pressure logic must check lifecycle state.
- Drain semantics per ADR-028 (two-valued signal, unknown ≠ drained, fail-open, 409-in-window deliberate).
